Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. The results indicate that the TV-PARX model consistently outperforms existing dynamic count models, exhibiting improved forecasting accuracy and flexibility in capturing data dynamics. As the TV-PARX model offers substantial advantages over existing time series models, we strongly recommend its use for analyzing and predicting count-based time series data sets.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems. 
A computational study is conducted to compare the practicalness of SISO-OFDM, MISO-OFDM, and our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1]. 
Results show that SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems can serve as viable alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1], and that SISO-OFDM systems outperform MISO-OFDM systems in terms of sum-throughput. 
Furthermore, SISO-OFDM systems can achieve similar fair-throughputs to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1], and have better coverage area performance. 
A real-world scenario is also demonstrated to illustrate the application of SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems in filling coverage gaps. 
By leveraging real-world macro base station data, we show that multiple SISO-OFDM systems can serve as effective fillers to fill coverage gaps left by a single wideband waveforming base station, and that such a setup can lead to substantial throughput gains. 
For instance, in a scenario with a single wideband waveforming base station located at 2.6GHz, multiple SISO-OFDM systems at 3.5GHz can fill coverage gaps and lead to an approximately 50\% throughput increase. 
In another scenario with a single wideband waveforming base station located at 3.5GHz, multiple SISO-OFDM systems at 3.8GHz can fill coverage gaps and lead to an approximately 60\% throughput increase. 
A comparative study is conducted to evaluate the throughput performance of SISO-OFDM, MISO-OFDM, and our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1] in a real-world scenario with multiple base stations. 
Results show that SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems can serve as strong alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1], and that SISO-OFDM systems outperform MISO-OFDM systems in terms of sum-throughput.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. A positive solution has been found for an edge-free arrangement existing after breaking at most three nodes for any bipartite graph, demonstrating that an edge-free visualization can be created even if pre-existing node characteristics aren't suitable. This optimization method varies from established techniques for using multiple connected components or splitting nodes pre-existing in complicated situations, due to its linear time complexity in relation to the total number of nodes split. This approach can be applied in various scenarios, including finding the minimum number of nodes required to split in order to draw a specific bipartite graph as a multiple-colored circle, reconnecting separated components to draw a highly interconnected bipartite graph, and determining if a bipartite graph represents a schedule feasible for a given set of sports events.

A computational method has been established to calculate a cooperative equilibrium through learning within the set of linear policy options. An empirical investigation was conducted to assess the predictive capability of this model by analyzing the pattern of cooperation in a variety of uniform distribution scenarios. With multiple uniform distributions, the system can achieve optimal cooperation when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. The code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhouyl1995/Contrastive-Feature-Extraction.

One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs. Furthermore, our research identifies a crucial constraint in the current knowledge graph embedding methodology that needs to be addressed. To address this constraint, we propose an alternative methodology based on the set theory. Our results confirm that this alternative approach results in better performance compared to the current standard. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the representation of posterior probabilities for different theories, employing both simple and more complicated examples for illustration. Ultimately, we outline a clear, step-by-step process for cognitive scientists to evaluate the reliability of Bayes factor analysis outcomes and ensure the trustworthiness of utility function choices. We further discuss the importance of open-source computational codes and the availability of empirical data to facilitate the reproduction of findings and promote widespread utilization of Bayes factor analysis. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. We present a clear, step-by-step explanation of the mentioned theory, along with illustrative examples to demonstrate the application of these conditions. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the aforementioned result, offering a new perspective by utilizing the fractional-order system's properties to deduce the inevitability of the outcome. We also offer a translation guide to help with the understanding of the used notation between the article and the relevant mathematical texts. We conclude by outlining the unmet requirements for the preservation of invariant curves in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems, presenting potential avenues for future research.
